OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice. Eastern Iran was partially reopened for overflights in June 2026 while the western part remains closed; very few international operators are using the FIR, with most Europe-Asia traffic routing south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. The shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in Jan 2020 illustrates how quickly misidentification risk can materialise.

cross.detail: Some overflights above FL285 are possible via specific temporary routes linking Oman/UAE with Central Asia, the Caucasus and Turkey, but western Iran remains heavily restricted. Several radar systems remain degraded, many western airports are still closed or daytime-only, and most operators continue avoiding the airspace.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the OIIX/Tehran FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Iran has previously conducted missile activity close to busy international routes with little warning. Major events: July 2026: EASA's current CZIB continues. June 2026: Eastern OIIX partially reopened; western part remains closed. March 2026: OIIX closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes on Iranian military targets and subsequent Iranian missile and drone retaliation. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed warnings. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other. Jan 2020: Iran shot down Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran after misidentifying the aircraft as a hostile target.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone. Iraq itself is open for overflights following the US-Iran ceasefire in June 2026, but most Europe-Asia traffic still routes south via Egypt/Saudi/Oman or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. The primary risks are missile and drone activity, misidentification by air-defence systems, and the ongoing threat from terrorist groups possessing portable anti-aircraft weaponry.

cross.detail: Iraq is open for overflights again, but its reopening does not restore the old Europe-Asia corridor because western Iran remains restricted and most operators still consider the ORBB/Baghdad FIR too high risk. Some airlines are using it, but the main flows remain north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan or south via Egypt/Saudi/Oman.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the ORBB/Baghdad FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Major events: July 2026: EASA's current CZIB continues. June 2026: ORBB reopened to overflights following the ceasefire, with north-south routes available. March 2026: ORBB closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation. June 2025: Airspace closed following Israeli missile attack on Iran; missiles and drones transited Iraqi airspace. Apr 2024: Airspace closed due to Iran drone and missile strike on Israel. Apr 2023: Drone and missile attacks in northern Iraq launched from Turkey and Iran, including strikes near ORSU and ORER. Oct 2021: US operators permitted to overfly ORBB above FL320 under updated FAA restrictions.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continue, and most international operators continue to avoid the OLBB/Beirut FIR. The primary risks are military activity linked to the Israel-Hezbollah conflict and the wider regional situation, including missile and drone activity. EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the OLBB/Beirut FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Some states allow limited operations to OLBA/Beirut provided arrivals and departures remain over the Mediterranean Sea. Major events: July 2026: EASA's current CZIB continues. Feb-Jul 2026: Israeli airstrikes continued in Lebanon despite repeated ceasefire extensions. Oct 2024: Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. Nov 2023 - ongoing: GNSS spoofing and jamming reported in the OLBB/Beirut FIR.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity. EASA has issued an Information Note advising operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR.

cross.detail: Open and operating normally. In practice, still not a major transit route for Europe-Asia traffic; most operators continue to route via Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. The OJAC/Amman FIR remains open and operating normally. The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts; Jordan has previously been affected by missiles and drones crossing its airspace during escalations involving Israel and Iran. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new Information Note advising operators to account for potential risk in the OJAC/Amman FIR following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: Jordan remained open throughout the Iran conflict, although missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries. Apr 2024: Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel. Oct 2023: Jordan intercepted drones and missiles transiting its airspace during regional escalation.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response. The OKAC/Kuwait FIR is currently open for arrivals and departures only — overflights remain prohibited — with restrictions extended until at least 4 August. Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport in March 2026.

cross.detail: Kuwait has extended its airspace restrictions until at least Aug 4. Overflights through the OKAC/Kuwait FIR are still not permitted; only flights arriving to or departing from OKKK/Kuwait are allowed, with prior approval.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait has been directly affected by the conflict. EASA advises operators not to operate in the OKAC/Kuwait FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB for the OKAC/Kuwait FIR. Feb-Jul 2026: OKAC closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict; currently open for arrivals and departures only, with overflights prohibited. March 2026: Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes across the region.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR. Bahrain is currently open to overflights, though nearby airspace — especially Kuwait — remains restricted. Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states in March 2026, with incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain.

cross.detail: Bahrain is open to overflights again. Note that nearby airspace, especially Kuwait, is still restricted and can affect routing. EASA advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. The OBBB/Bahrain FIR remains open to overflights. EASA advises operators not to operate in the OBBB/Bahrain FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB for the OBBB/Bahrain FIR. Feb-Jul 2026: OBBB closed and reopened several times before returning to normal overflight operations. March 2026: Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states, with incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation — including a missile strike near Al Udeid Air Base in March 2026 — keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease. The OTDF/Doha FIR is currently open and operating largely normally.

cross.detail: Qatar has now reopened to overflights. Earlier restrictions on waypoints and arrival/departure route segments have been withdrawn, although some temporary restricted areas and military activity remain. EASA advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. The OTDF/Doha FIR remains open and operating largely normally. EASA advises operators not to operate in the OTDF/Doha FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB for the OTDF/Doha FIR. Feb-Jul 2026: OTDF closed and reopened several times before returning to normal overflight operations. March 2026: Iranian missile strike reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy. The FIR remains open to overflights, with traffic managed through normal ATS routes and temporary RNAV corridors; GPS interference continues to be a significant operational issue across the FIR.

cross.detail: The UAE remains open to overflights, with traffic managed through a mixture of normal ATS routes and temporary RNAV corridors. GPS interference continues to be one of the biggest operational issues across the FIR. EASA advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate. Oman remains open and is a key part of the southern bypass route used by Europe-Asia traffic, carrying significant overflight traffic via the Egypt-Saudi-Oman corridor. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E.

cross.detail: Oman remains one of the most useful FIRs in the region for the southern bypass. It is open but still part of the managed corridor system, with flow measures and ongoing GNSS interference reports.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. The OOMM/Muscat FIR remains open. The primary risk is spillover of missile or drone activity from conflicts elsewhere in the region. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E. Feb-Jul 2026: Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the Gulf region. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other, leading many operators to avoid airspace between the two countries.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it. The primary risks include military activity linked to the Syrian conflict, Israeli airstrikes targeting Iranian and Hezbollah-linked positions, and the potential for misidentification by air-defence systems.

cross.detail: Syria has quietly become part of the regional routing picture again after years of almost no international overflight traffic.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. The OSTT/Damascus FIR remains high risk, but some regional operators have started using it as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq routing. Several countries continue to prohibit or advise against operations in OSTT due to risk from military operations, anti-aviation weaponry and unstable security conditions. Major events: March 2026: OSTT closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation. Jan-Jul 2026: Gradual increase in overflights through Syria as some regional operators use the FIR as an alternative to Iran and Iraq. Dec 2024: Syrian airspace temporarily closed following the fall of the Assad regime. Oct 2023: Airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo airports. Feb 2020: An A320 approaching Damascus diverted after being caught in crossfire during Israeli airstrikes. Sep 2018: Russian IL-20 shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017.

cross.detail: Yemen remains an active conflict zone, and the vast majority of Yemeni airspace (OYSC/Sanaa FIR) should be avoided. Several countries prohibit aircraft from overflying any land portion of the FIR. US operators can still use offshore routes UT702 and M999, while other countries permit flights on overwater portions of Yemeni airspace. Saudi airspace to the north and Somali airspace to the south also have risks. The primary risk is intentional targeting by terrorist groups with access to sophisticated anti-aircraft weaponry. Civil aircraft may also be endangered by ongoing high-intensity military operations including explosive drones and missiles. Saudi and Israeli airstrikes can occur at any time, including in the capital Sana'a. Major events: Jul 2026: Yemen's government carried out an airstrike on the runway at OYSN/Sanaa Airport to stop an Iranian aircraft from landing. Dec 2024 - ongoing: OYSN/Sanaa Airport closed due to damage from Israeli airstrikes in Dec 2024 and May 2025. Jan 2024: US and UK carried out airstrikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen, in response to missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. Sep 2023: Houthi drone attacks near the Yemen-Saudi border. Apr-Oct 2022: All parties in the Yemeni conflict agreed a ceasefire. 2018-2022: Frequent Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa and other targets in Yemen in retaliation for Houthi drone attacks across the border. 2017: OYSN/Sanaa Airport badly damaged by coalition airstrikes.

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference. Drone attacks across Russia have been ramping up since June 2025, reaching as far as Siberia; hundreds have been shot down — including near Moscow — using surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes. Disruptions now occur by day as well as night. Most operators avoid Russian airspace completely, but those still transiting should be prepared for sudden closures or reroutes.

cross.detail: Ukraine's airspace has remained fully closed to civil aviation since the Russian invasion in Feb 2022. Large parts of Russian airspace near the Ukraine border have also remained restricted. Several countries prohibit their operators from using Russian airspace near the FIR boundaries with Ukraine. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military near the Russia-Ukraine border, including misidentification. Major events: Jan 2025: EASA issued a new CZIB recommending against flights in western Russia (anywhere west of 60 deg E) due to misidentification risk from air-defence systems targeting Ukrainian drones and missiles, following the shoot-down of a passenger jet at URMG/Grozny on Dec 25. Jan 2024: Crash of military transport aircraft near Belgarod, approx 20nm from the Ukrainian border; Russia and Ukraine each accused the other of shooting it down. Aug 2023: Private jet carrying Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin crashed en route from Moscow to St Petersburg on Aug 23. July 2023 - ongoing: Drone strikes on targets in Moscow and surrounding region, with Moscow airports forced to close temporarily on multiple occasions, becoming more frequent.

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM.

cross.detail: Ukraine closed its entire airspace to all civil traffic on Feb 24, 2022, due to a military invasion by Russia. There is an ongoing active conflict between Russian and Ukrainian forces. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of their own airspace near their FIR boundaries with Ukraine. All major countries that regularly issue airspace warnings (the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy) have issued total flight bans for Ukraine due to risk from military activity at all levels. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military, including misidentification. The secondary risk is potential loss of Ukrainian ATC service at short notice (e.g. cyber attack) and other unforeseeable non-normal operating environments. Prior to February 2022, two areas of concern existed in Ukraine: the conflict in the far east (affecting UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the airspace authority dispute over Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits.

cross.detail: Following a military coup in April 2023, Sudan remains closed to all civilian flights. In South Sudan, air navigation services remain suspended above FL245. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed, but no NOTAMs are being issued. A contingency plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. Several countries have issued airspace warnings advising operators not to enter Sudanese airspace due to risks from anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity. The primary risk is security on the ground for any unplanned diversions; throughout the conflict, passenger jets have been targeted by gunfire at HSSK/Khartoum Airport. The secondary risk is Sudan's proximity to South Sudan, which has poor ATC provision below FL245. Major events: Nov 2025: Il-76 reportedly shot down by a surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan. May 2025: Drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. Oct 2024: Foreign-registered cargo aircraft shot down by local militia over North Darfur, near the border with Chad. Apr 2023: Military coup on Apr 15; Sudan's airspace closed, South Sudan's airspace closed above FL245. Oct 2021: Military coup on Oct 25; HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days with all flights suspended.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: A civil war has been ongoing since 2014. Some progress was made in Oct 2020 with the formation of a new government, but Libya remains an active conflict zone with armed clashes between rival militia groups. Libyan airspace (HLLL/Tripoli FIR) should be avoided entirely. A total flight ban applies for US operators, and several other countries have warnings in place. The primary risk is misidentification by Libyan air-defence systems, or by militia who have threatened to shoot down aircraft operating in western Libya, including at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity has been reported over the high seas, either as OAT or not in contact with ATC. The secondary risk is that reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed, with regular ATS and radar outages and severe VHF limitations across the HLLL FIR. Major events: August 2023: Major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. July 2023: Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya. Aug 2022: Militia air-defence forces claimed to have shot down a US drone near Benghazi during increased tensions between competing militias. June 2022: Failed militia attempt to seize Tripoli government offices resulted in armed clashes and suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga airport. Jan 2020: Multiple airstrikes targeting HLLM/Mitiga airport. Nov 2019: Militia advancing on Tripoli declared a no-fly-zone around the city, threatening to shoot down civil aircraft attempting to fly to HLLM/Mitiga airport. 2014: HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after clashes between rival militias; most flights now operate from HLLM/Mitiga airport.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban.

cross.detail: The conflict in northern and central Mali has continued since 2012 and the security situation remains volatile. Several countries have airspace warnings in place, typically advising operations at or above FL250 or FL260 and avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal. The US advises caution in Mali airspace at all levels due to ongoing fighting, expanding militant activity, and the presence of a state-run paramilitary force operating anti-aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. The primary risks include MANPADS and other surface-to-air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and the potential for misidentification or spillover from military activity. Low-level and airport-phase operations carry the highest exposure. ATS in Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs, which have a long-standing restriction for overflights of Mali to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. Major events: April 2026: The security situation escalated sharply, with coordinated attacks nationwide against state and military targets on April 25, including gunfire and explosions near GABS/Bamako. France issued a new airspace warning advising French operators not to operate to/from GABS or use it as an alternate. Sep 2024: Insurgents breached GABS/Bamako and set the presidential jet on fire; the airport closed temporarily. Dec 2023: Germany prohibited its operators below FL260 in northern Mali; commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu were cancelled after shelling near the airport, and a military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao with reports it may have been shot down. Aug 2020: All airports closed for two days during a military coup; Bamako ACC remained operational and overflights were unaffected. Apr 2018: Militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu using indirect fire and vehicle bombs. Jan 2017 and Nov 2016: Vehicle bomb and rocket attacks targeted GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali.

cross.detail: The situation on the ground is highly unstable with ongoing attacks from extremist militants showing intent to target aviation interests. The primary risk is to overflying aircraft at lower flight levels, which may be targeted by anti-aircraft-capable weapons. The US prohibits flights across the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR below FL260, except for flights transiting the overwater portion going to/from HDAM/Djibouti. Several other countries advise against operating below FL260. A secondary risk comes from unauthorised ATC units issuing climb/descent instructions conflicting with official ones from Mogadishu Control. From Nov 2025, an authority dispute has emerged in the north of the FIR: Somaliland requires a PPR from its own CAA for all overflights, while Somalia has reaffirmed through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR — expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia. Major events: Feb 2024: Reports of aircraft within the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR being contacted by a fake controller on the same frequency, issuing conflicting instructions. Aug 2023: Reports of uncontrolled operations including combat helicopters flying at low levels (FL030) not reporting position, altitude or routing. Oct 2022: The Somalian government warned that HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups. May 2022: Class A airspace implemented in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR above FL245. 2020-ongoing: Multiple Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets, including a UN compound. May 2020: An Embraer EMB-120 was shot down on approach to Bardale airstrip, killing all six on board — an accidental shoot-down by Ethiopian forces combating Al-Shabaab.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. In May 2025 there was a period of intense cross-border shelling and aerial activity in Kashmir; a ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held, but the situation remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance, generally advising operators to remain at or above FL260. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including potential MANPADS below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in the Kashmir region; ceasefire announced on 10 May. Some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. In May 2025 there was a period of intense cross-border shelling and aerial activity in Kashmir; a ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held, but the situation remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance, generally advising operators to remain at or above FL260. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including potential MANPADS below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in the Kashmir region; ceasefire announced on 10 May. Some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances. Traffic through the FIR increased in early 2026 as flights sought a northern bypass around the closed central Middle East corridor following US and Israeli strikes on Iran.

cross.detail: The OAKX/Kabul FIR remains Class G with no normal ATS service; crews still need to use the published contingency routes and operate with TIBA procedures. Armenia and Azerbaijan remain important parts of the northern bypass, with steady overflight demand.

March 2026: The OAKX/Kabul FIR remains open but has no ATC service — it is uncontrolled Class G airspace following the US and allied withdrawal in Aug 2021. Some countries restrict overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR; others allow overflights across the entire airspace at and above FL320. The primary risk is surface-to-air fire at low altitudes, with no ATC service and an extreme threat to aircraft and crew on the ground. Major events: March 2026: Traffic increased through OAKX as flights used the northern bypass around the closed Middle East corridor. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; commercial traffic continued to transit the FIR via P500 and G500. Aug 2021: US and allied forces withdrew from Afghanistan; OAKX became uncontrolled Class G airspace with no ATC service.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The airspace risk picture in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region (the Ethiopia/Eritrea border) has been improving since a peace deal was agreed in early Nov 2022. Airspace warnings remain in place, however, with several states advising avoidance of the area. The primary risk is from large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry that could affect overflights — whether through misidentification or being caught in crossfire. Major events: Feb 2024: New flare-up in fighting in the Amhara region (south of Tigray), including airstrikes. Nov 2022: Peace deal agreed in the Tigray region; Ethiopian Airlines planned to resume flights to HAMK/Mekele airport. Nov 2021: Several western countries issued airspace warnings and do-not-travel advisories for the Tigray region following increased fighting. July 2021: HAAA/Addis FIR published a NOTAM closing a section of airspace below FL290 over Tigray, following reports that militia shot down a military transport near HAMK/Mekele. Nov 2020: Major escalation of conflict in the Tigray region; some airways closed by Ethiopian and Sudanese CAAs; UN321, UG300 and UL432 were close to the conflict zone. Multiple airports were targeted by rockets; missiles were fired into Eritrea targeting HHAS/Asmara; HABD/Bahir Dar and HAGN/Gondar were also targeted. Sep 2018: Ethiopian ATC controllers went on strike; the ECAA and Ethiopian Airlines recruited retired and foreign controllers, some not qualified to operate in Ethiopian airspace.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The security situation in Myanmar has deteriorated since the military coup in Feb 2021, with conflict and violence across many parts of the country involving airstrikes and armed clashes. Several countries have issued airspace warnings at lower flight levels due to risk from military operations, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. GPS jamming has also been reported in the north of the FIR on overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace. Major events: Jan 2024: Armed group shot down a military helicopter in the northern state of Kachin, likely using a MANPADS. Sep 2023: Several attacks by rebel groups against military targets, including a makeshift drone dropping bombs on aircraft hangars at an airbase next to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport. Sep 2023: Reports of intermittent GPS jamming on airway N895 over the mainland in the VYYF/Yangon FIR. Apr 2023: VYYY/Yangon airport temporarily closed following an attack by resistance groups with improvised artillery rounds. Sep 2022: A Myanmar National Airlines passenger was reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of an ATR 72 on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. Feb 2021: Military coup ousted the government; an ATC strike at the end of Feb resulted in no ATC service for overflights, followed by increasing strikes, mass protests and armed clashes.
